title: The library's quiet first hour
paragraphs: When Bukit Ria Library reopened its upstairs reading room, staff introduced a Quiet First Hour on Saturday mornings. Several students had asked for a place to read before weekend activities began, while some older visitors said that amplified phone calls made concentration difficult. For the first hour after opening, calls were directed to the lobby and conversation in the reading room was kept brief. The rest of the library operated normally.

The arrangement was deliberately modest. Floor signs explained the hour in Malay, English and Indonesian, and staff offered headphones to visitors watching videos. Children's programmes and group study continued downstairs. Head librarian Suri Anwar said the aim was not to make the whole building silent, but to test whether one predictable period could serve readers who needed sustained attention.

On the first morning, only eighteen people used the upstairs room. By the sixth Saturday, forty-seven people entered during the quiet hour, and book loans made from the room rose from twenty-three to fifty-one. In an anonymous card survey, thirty-one of thirty-nine respondents said that they found it easier to concentrate there. A few visitors began waiting outside before the doors opened; once inside, even newcomers tended to soften their footsteps without being reminded.

Those figures are encouraging, although they do not settle every question. The later Saturdays fell close to school examinations, when demand for study space usually rises, and the survey represented visitors who had chosen to use the room. Two parents also worried that families arriving early might feel unwelcome if children spoke. In response, staff placed a clearly marked conversation area near the upstairs entrance and added picture cards explaining where livelier activities were available.

The library has extended the trial for two months and will compare attendance after examinations end. It will also invite feedback from visitors who avoid the quiet hour, not only those who use it. The experiment has already shown that a limited quiet period can attract readers without silencing the entire library. Still, as Anwar observed, it is a small service worth refining, not proof that one arrangement will suit every visitor.
